title: Reconciliation in Christ
english: We once knew Christ according to the flesh, but now we know him no longer in that way. For though he lived a human life, he rose after three days and now lives toward the Father in heaven, so he is to be understood not merely in bodily terms but above the flesh. Indeed, having died once, he dies no more; death has no dominion over him. He died to sin once for all, and the life he now lives he lives to God. Therefore, if he who is the author of our life has entered into this state, we too must follow in his steps—not remaining in the flesh, but being understood above it.

Justly has the divine Paul spoken. For if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: the old has passed away, behold, the new has come. The old is what Scripture says: 'You are dust, and to dust you shall return.' It is also the tendency of the human mind toward evil from youth, as written in Moses. And indeed, the old includes all that is in the law. But now we are to regard all these things as passed away.

For we have been justified by faith in Christ, and the power of the curse has been broken. He who once brought death into power has now lived again on our behalf, and we have come to know the true and essential God. We worship him in spirit and in truth, as the Son mediates and pours out upon the world the blessings from the Father above. Therefore, as the divine Paul declares wisely, all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ.
And truly, this mystery of God’s economy with regard to the flesh is not unwilling to the Father, but the renewal that comes through him is pleasing to him.

The mystagogue adds that the Father himself reconciled us to himself through Christ, we who had become his enemies through our wandering into polytheism—Greeks lost in much-god delusion, Jews fallen upon the shadows of the law, and not applying ourselves to the true worship. Through him we have obtained access, and as he himself says, 'No one comes to the Father except through him.' Therefore all things are from God, who reconciled us through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation.

Attend again to this: Christ gave them the ministry of reconciliation, for they have been ordained through him to apostleship—God said it, the One who gave. Therefore they declare him equal to the Father, knowing one lordship and authority belonging to both. Who then is this, what is this word upon the ministry, or what is the manner of the reconciliation? He brings forward, saying, 'God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself,' that is, the One in Christ reconciling the world to himself—God was. Through faith, as I said, into Christ, we have been at peace with God, that is, we have been reconciled. And of this a clear demonstration is the forgiveness of those who have sinned, which God graciously gives as both God and Father.

Again he insists upon authority as God the Son, saying to the paralytic, 'Your sins are forgiven you.' Therefore in Christ, that is, in the person of Christ, God reconciles the world to himself, not reckoning to those who have sinned their transgressions. Since moreover we have been appointed, he says, to the priesthood of the evangelical decrees, and the word of reconciliation has been placed in us.

We are God’s servants, and therefore we necessarily offer prayers on behalf of those who have believed in this manner, taking up, as it were, the very face of Christ. To those who wish to depart, we say: We beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God, having believed in him. It is clear that the one on whose behalf we act as ambassadors is none other than Christ himself.

For Christ is the door and he himself is the way. Since it was likely that some would regard the evangelical proclamations as illogical, and consider the truly acceptable time of salvation as nothing, and would be pushed aside and afterward abandon the faith, the mystagogue again thinks of something for them—not unconquerably having toward shame, and toward easily persuading them not to…

title: Spiritual Warfare and the Armor of God
english: Their turning toward God. For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh, since the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly but mighty through God to overthrow strongholds. Those who seek glory in battle and oppose their enemies in a carnal way would naturally possess carnal armor—helmet, breastplate, weapons, swords, and whatever tools they need to conquer—but our warfare demands spiritual weapons, as the inspired Paul declares.

He declares that the soldier imagined in Christ must be clothed in these splendid armaments: a breastplate of righteousness, a helmet of salvation, the sword of the Spirit which is the word of God, and the shield of faith, by which all the fiery darts of the evil one are extinguished. Therefore the weapons of the saints are not carnal but spiritual and powerful through God, effective for tearing down fortifications—not only of Hellenic doctrines and heresies but also for exposing their reasonings as hostile, unskilled, and foolishly woven.

Therefore let us tear down such strongholds and every proud idea that rises up against the knowledge of God. Let us take every thought captive to obey Christ, instead of overthrowing every idea that exalts itself against God in impious thoughts; let us praise Him with fitting voices, never imagining anything lowly about Him.

He helpfully brings up those who, from an excess of simplicity, imagined Christ to be truly weak, thinking that his endurance of the cross and his bearing of the Jews' shamelessness—or impiety—proved it. In defense, he places before us at the right moment the power of the mystery, explaining the voluntary self-emptying of the Only-begotten and the surpassing glory that followed.

Indeed, he says, those who imagine they still have far to go in faith suppose, according to their own view, that Christ was crucified from weakness, suffered as a man, and willingly endured the death of the flesh. But it is necessary to know this as well: having despoiled Hades and bound the power of death, he rose again on the third day—not by human strength, but by divine and ineffable power.
